entries.title: Why a Popular Push to Ban Congressional Stock Trading Crashed and Burned
entries.summary: But is it only mostly dead?
entries.content:
Conservative or liberal, Republican or Democrat, an overwhelming majority of Americans want members of Congress to stop trading individual stocks.

But on Wednesday, after months of legislative momentum toward a measure designed to fight insider trading, curb conflicts of interest and stop rampant violations of existing financial disclosure laws, Congress’ best shot this decade at a stock-ban law died unceremoniously in the Senate during a party-line procedural vote.

So why did such an uncommonly popular measure unravel so abruptly?

Fundamentally, this week’s failure is the culmination of a decade’s worth of discarded political opportunities and partisan ill will. In public statements and campaign ads, many members of Congress from both parties say they’re staunchly opposed to congressional stock trading. But despite a real opportunity to legislate changes, they didn’t deliver.

The contemporary push for a congressional stock-trading ban began in earnest during 2021.

Democrats enjoyed a rare Washington power trifecta, controlling the White House, House and Senate. They were keen to fix what they considered a post-Trump political system eroded by self-interest and drowned in big money. COVID-era accusations of insider trading against several senators rocked Capitol Hill. So, too, did stock investment disclosure scandals involving lawmakers such as then-Rep. Tom Malinowski (D-New Jersey).

But then-House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, who Republicans have made a sort of avatar for stock-trading excess because of her husband’s massive stock sales and purchases, resisted.

A Pelosi-controlled committee declined to attach stock-ban language to a larger ethics bill known as H.R. 1. Pelosi rejected a stock trading ban, declaring: “We are a free-market economy.” She later softened her stance after pressure from her party. But weeks before Republicans were set to assume control of the House, Pelosi let an active and actionable stock-ban bill die in December 2022.

Meanwhile, dozens of federal lawmakers kept violating the existing Stop Trading on Congressional Knowledge Act of 2012, a bipartisan, Obama-era law that was supposed to keep elected officials from using their public perch to pad their personal finances.

Democrats and Republicans alike kept skirting the STOCK Act, and that’s no statement of false equivalence, as social media scolds so often cry. Republican and Democratic lawmakers have violated the STOCK Act’s disclosure provisions on a nearly 1-to-1 basis this decade, a Washington Sun analysis indicates.“Part of this is compliance with the law, and part of this is the idea that shame is gone,” said Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz, who as a member of Congress introduced the House’s version of the STOCK Act. “All of this stuff undermines faith in government.”

Should everyone in Congress now simply stop trading individual stocks?

“Absolutely. One-hundred percent,” Walz told The Sun recently. “If you’re going to run for office, you shouldn’t do it.”

Meanwhile, apparent financial conflicts of interest continued unabated. Members of the House and Senate armed services committees traded defense-contractor stocks. Members of financial committees traded financial stocks. Lawmakers championing health care legislation bought and sold shares of pharmaceutical and medical tech companies.After stock-ban false starts during 2023 and 2024, lawmakers reenergized debate last year, motivated in part to rehabilitate Congress’ historically dismal approval rating, which many considered self-inflicted — from accusations of sexual misconduct to bribery to fraud to various flavors of personal enrichment.

Several current and former prolific stock-trading House members — Julie Johnson (D-Texas), Rob Bresnahan (R-Pennsylvania), Val Demings (D-Oregon), Jefferson Shreve (R-Indiana), Kelly Morrison (D-Minnesota) — chose to quit cold turkey after enduring criticism and scrutiny.

The Republican-led Senate passed one stock ban bill out of committee in July 2025. Several bipartisan House efforts stalled out, particularly those that sought to squelch President Donald Trump’s stock-trading habits or otherwise involve the executive branch. But House Speaker Mike Johnson, at times a stock-ban skeptic, endorsed the leadership-backed Stop Insider Trading Act in early 2026. Trump blessed the bill during his State of the Union address in February.

The Republican-controlled House did something in July that no Democratic-led chamber achieved: It passed a stock-ban bill on an up-and-down vote, 232-198, with 13 Democrats joining all Republicans.

But the Stop Insider Trading Act ran into two roadblocks in the Senate that kept the chamber from sending the measure to Trump’s desk.

The first: Republicans’ insistence on tying it to a national voter identification requirement, a nonstarter for Democrats.

The second: Loopholes in the bill that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer described as “swiss-cheese legislating.” For example, it allowed lawmakers to continue holding and selling stocks they already own. Republicans largely scoffed at this argument, with Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Nebraska) lamenting Wednesday that “Senate Democrats refused to support this commonsense bill” that would have “tackled insider trading to rebuild public trust and make sure Congress plays by the rules.”

The Stop Insider Trading Act’s failure means the STOCK Act remains unchanged. In dozens of interviews with The Washington Sun during the past year, Democratic and Republican lawmakers and operatives alike generally agreed that the law’s ineffectiveness and lawmakers’ habitual noncompliance stem from a lack of consequences and enforcement.

A few members of Congress have simply ignored STOCK Act requirements or those of the related Ethics in Government Act. Violation fines — $200 for a first-time offender — border on comical, mere pocket change for elected officials who often measure their personal wealth in seven, eight or even nine figures. Even Rep. Michael Guest (R-Mississippi), the House Ethics Committee chairman charged with overseeing STOCK Act compliance, violated the STOCK Act in August.

And in the 14 years since its passage, there’s never been a STOCK Act-related criminal prosecution.

Could a congressional stock ban be resurrected after the midterm elections?

With less than three months between the midterms and the start of the new Congress, a fresh push to pass the stock-trading ban would face the same partisan obstacles as it did before. That could leave the issue for the next class of lawmakers to take up in 2027.

entries.title: White House Premieres a New Taxpayer-Funded Ad Lauding the Iran War
entries.summary: The Trump administration has spent millions on campaign-style ad spots over the last week.
entries.content:
U.S. taxpayers funded another high-octane, government-sponsored ad across cable news channels premiering Wednesday night, this time promoting President Donald Trump’s war with Iran.

The spot, first flagged by political ad-buying firm Medium Buying, flaunts a flashing series of missile strikes and F-22 jet acrobatics interlaced over bombastic speech from Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

“This regime will soon learn that no one should challenge the strength and might of the United States armed forces,” Trump narrates.

Trump’s military conflict in Iran has been deeply unpopular with the American public: Polls consistently find that less than a third of Americans support the war.

Also unpopular, at least among Washington lawmakers, is the White House’s recent decision to spend millions in taxpayer dollars on midterm advertisements. Republican and Democratic lawmakers have criticized the Trump administration’s recent ad spending as potentially illegal and a misuse of taxpayer funds. Senate Majority Leader John Thune this week called them “a great message” that “shouldn’t be paid for by taxpayer dollars.”

The White House transferred $20 million in Homeland Security funds to bankroll the ads, including one earlier this week that was similar to a 2024 Trump campaign ad.

Reporters asked the president Wednesday about whether the ads, which began running last week, may in fact violate federal anti-propaganda laws. He brushed off concerns and suggested the spots are meant to promote the country rather than his own political interests.

“I’m not promoting myself because I’m not running for office,” he said. “I’m promoting the country.”

A few hours before, the Federal Communications Commission said that taxpayer-funded television ads featuring the president do not raise any red flags.

"There's nothing in there that strikes me to merit any sort of FCC review or any liability for any broadcaster for running a regular, normal PSA ad," said FCC Chair Brendan ⁠Carr, a Trump appointee.

entries.title: The Mystics' Season Is Over After Their Game 2 Loss to Atlanta
entries.summary: Washington, which exceeded expectations this season as the youngest team in the WNBA, fell to the Dream on Wednesday, 93-75.
entries.content:
The Mystics’ season came to a close on Wednesday with a 93-75 loss to the Dream.

Washington never led in a choppy and occasionally ugly game, in which both teams combined for 53 fouls. The Mystics made several runs to keep it close and cut their deficit to as low as 3 points as late as the early fourth quarter. But they could never close the gap.

This was their first home playoff game since 2019 and first postseason series since 2023. It ended in a first-round sweep.

The Dream’s defense was ultimately too much for the Mystics to overcome. Atlanta once again pressured Washington into a series of costly turnovers early. (Although the Mystics cut down on their 23 turnovers from Game 1, they still finished with 19, while forcing just eight.) Their offense found themselves consistently pressed into bad looks and awkward shots. Even in the paint, where they usually thrive, Washington could do relatively little.

Sonia Citron led the Mystics in scoring with 25 points. Kiki Iriafen added 15 points and 16 rebounds.

It ends a joyful, surprisingly successful season for the Mystics. With some impressive developmental leaps among their young players, the team's rebuild ended ahead of schedule, and they became the youngest roster to qualify for the playoffs in the history of the WNBA.

entries.title: D.C. Residents Push Back on RFK Stadium Master Plan
entries.summary: Testimony revealed deep anxieties over massive parking structures, transit gaps and environmental protections surrounding the 180-acre campus.
entries.content:
Mayor Muriel Bowser’s new $3.8 billion blueprint to transform the RFK Stadium campus is facing intense community opposition.

Residents who would soon live next to the new home of the Washington Commanders are deeply concerned over potential traffic impacts, community displacement and pollution. After months of community meetings, that mounting frustration spilled into the Wilson Building on Wednesday.

D.C. Council members heard from dozens of residents and community advocates during a hearing on the finalized master plan for the 180-acre site, which Bowser sent to the legislature last week. With a final vote expected later this year, residents made clear that they expect lawmakers to step in and alter the plan before it crosses the finish line.

The proposal anchors a 65,000-seat stadium for the Commanders alongside up to 6,500 homes, commercial space and new parks. But residents living in the immediate shadow of the site in Ward 7 and the historic Kingman Park neighborhood said they fear the plan’s massive footprint and game-day logistics will overwhelm their communities.

“It is unclear to me why the city can invest so much time and effort into creating these structures — for a lot of people who probably don’t live here — and we get stuck with the aftereffects, which are not assets to our neighborhood,” Sarah Miller, a Ward 7 resident who lives just blocks from the site, said at the council meeting.

That anxiety was echoed from the dais.

“I do not want to find ourselves in a situation 30 years from now asking ourselves, ‘Did we get this right?’” Ward 7 council member Wendell Felder said to open the hearing. “Did we create the conditions that will help prevent displacement, or did we unintentionally contribute to it?”

Here are the dominant concerns driving the pushback.

The Parking Garage Behemoth 

No single element of the master plan drew more unified outrage than “Garage G2” — a massive parking structure planned for the north side of the stadium, slated to directly face Kingman Park.

Ebony Payne, the advisory neighborhood commissioner representing Kingman Park, noted that even though the Commanders scaled back plans for three parking garages in response to resident concerns after their first draft this summer, they are now proposing combining two of those garages into a single, nine-story monolith.

“Kingman Park is still slated to be in the receiving end of the largest parking garage ever built in D.C. history, with 3,600 parking spaces at nine stories high,” Payne said. “That will be as long as the Washington Monument if it was turned on its side.”

Project officials — including Brian Hanlon, D.C. Department of Buildings director and RFK project executive — defended the design and garage locations during Wednesday’s hearing. While some residents have pushed for the structures to be placed underground to minimize their visual and physical impact, subsurface parking is logistically prohibitive and drastically more expensive given the site’s high water table and proximity to underground Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority tunnels, Hanlon said.

Transit Gaps and Traffic Congestion

Tied directly to the parking footprint is the fear of gridlock around the campus. Ward 6 council member Charles Allen hammered this point during the hearing, noting the plans would result in the stadium operating with five times the number of structured garage parking spaces as Nationals Park.

“Anybody who tells you this is a transit-first stadium, just do not buy what they are selling,” Allen said.

The city has leaned on a proposed “Gold Line” rapid bus route along H Street and expansions to the existing Stadium-Armory Metro station, but residents argue the plan lacks the heavy public transit infrastructure required for a venue of this magnitude.

WMATA officials previously ruled out building a new infill Metrorail station due to cost and engineering constraints. Several community members on Wednesday argued that the decision should be reevaluated. Brian Alcorn, chair of ANC 7D, warned that relying on existing road networks will paralyze the surrounding area and pleaded for the eventual inclusion of a new Metro station.

Recalling the gridlock that frequently plagues Northwest Stadium in Landover on game days, Alcorn and other neighbors pleaded with the council not to create those miserable traffic circumstances in the District.

Fears of Gentrification and Displacement 

Longtime Ward 7 residents said the promise of the stadium campus and its amenities cannot be separated from the immediate threat of being priced out.

The Commanders have said they considered these concerns. At a council hearing earlier this week focused on the team’s $50 million community benefits package and stadium subsidy, Kirtan Mehta, the Commanders’ chief external affairs officer, said the franchise is “building not just a football stadium, but a neighborhood.”

During Wednesday’s hearing, Felder pointed to a $60 million community reinvestment fund established in addition to the team’s contributions, designed specifically to focus on displacement prevention like rental assistance and property tax relief for long-term homeowners.

But for neighbors like Laura Richards, the proposed neighborhood threatens to displace marginalized residents already living there. Richards called on the council to take concrete legislative action before breaking ground — such as an outright ban on the use of eminent domain in the surrounding census tracts.

“Now is the time to address what happens to those circumference neighborhoods,” Richards said. “Instead of waiting 30 years and saying, ‘Oh, what did we do wrong?’ You can stop it now.”

Climate Goals and Green Energy 

Environmental advocates urged the council to use its leverage to strengthen the project’s climate requirements, emphasizing concerns that the plan leaves the door open for fossil fuel combustion on the site.

Maurice Hall, a Ward 7 resident whose family has lived in the area for 50 years, urged the council to amend the master plan to explicitly prohibit combustion on the campus and commit to cleaner alternatives like solar or geothermal power.

“D.C. residents have contributed over a billion dollars to this project. If fossil fuels are allowed to burn on the site, we will have paid to poison our communities, including our parks, homes and schools,” Hall said.

The Pickleball Lobby

While megagarages and traffic congestion dominated the hearing, highly specific recreational demands also surfaced — most notably, the push for more pickleball.

Lana Duran, a local realtor and pickleball organizer, testified that the four courts currently allocated in the master plan fall drastically short of community demand as the sport increases in popularity. She was joined by several others in asking the council to mandate that the site include 24 dedicated pickleball courts in the final layout to host youth programs, leagues and tournaments.

Office of Planning Director Anita Cozart defended the pickleball plan as "commensurate with the very diverse array of recreational options that people articulated as priorities," adding the design remains "flexible."

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: The Very Hungry Guard
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 1, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

 In today’s newsletter: What it costs to feed the National Guard, the Circulator’s re-circulation and a federal crackdown on D.C. … mosquitoes.

Capital Weather's Daily Digit — 8/10. On the warm side, with highs well into the 80s. But we’re running low on warm days, so it's worth enjoying. Full forecast from Capital Weather.





THE LATEST

National Guard members have worked up a $49 million appetite patrolling D.C. over the past year, The Washington Sun’s Zara Norman reports.

That’s how much the Department of Defense has spent since October 2025 on catered “breakfast, lunch, dinner and midnight meals” for National Guard members deployed to D.C. as part of President Donald Trump’s Safe and Beautiful Task Force and Freedom 250 celebrations, according to government contracts reviewed by The Sun.

It’s the latest figure ratcheting up the estimated price tag on the Guard’s presence in D.C., which has been extended through the remainder of Trump’s term. The Congressional Budget Office has estimated the cost of deploying 1,000 troops to a city to be $18 million to $21 million a month (as of early August, there were 4,630 troops deployed to D.C.). It’ll cost $292 million to house troops in 2,000 “apartment-style lodging units” around the District through June 2027.

It looks like it will cost an additional $20 million to feed troops for the rest of this year, as one contract good through December has that amount unspent. Neither the National Guard nor the catering vendors it contracted with responded to questions about the contracts or any further catering costs the Guard will incur through January 2029.





DEEP DIVE

Questions were circulating in The Sun newsroom yesterday after our colleague Emily Kennard spotted a D.C. Circulator bus driving along Maryland Avenue NE.

You may remember the Circulator as the red buses that started carrying passengers in 2005, seeking to fill gaps in the service provided by Metro. At its peak, the Circulator buses — which served routes including around the National Mall, from Georgetown to Union Station and Congress Heights to Union Station — carried more than 5 million passengers a year.

The Circulator was killed off in late 2024, in part because ridership fell after the pandemic and the city entered a period of budget woes. The city sold off its stock of Circulator buses, with many ending up in far-flung locations like Boston, California and even the resort town of Stowe, Vermont.

But what of the rogue Circulator Emily spotted? Six Circulator buses did stay within the city’s government, though not as part of a secret fleet to restore passenger service. (Bummer.) Two went to D.C. Fire and Emergency Medical Services for use at its academy, one went to the Department of Youth Rehabilitation Services, and the remaining three landed at the Department of Employment Services.

The bus Emily saw was destined for the Infrastructure Academy, a new job training site at the old Spingarn High School building in Northeast and reopening today after a $73 million renovation. The academy has bus bays for students training to be bus and auto mechanics, a DOES spokesperson tells The Sun.

See something that you want us to dig into? Get in touch.





FROM THE DISTRICT

A marathon D.C. Council hearing on the $3.8 billion RFK Stadium master plan revealed deep community anxieties over massive parking garages, environmental impacts and the threat of displacement in Ward 7, The Sun’s Michael-Brice Saddler reports.

D.C. mosquitoes and ticks, be warned: The federal government is coming for you. The Sun’s Justice Covert reports that Trump signed an executive order this week directing federal agencies to work with local officials to reduce the city’s mosquito population by 90% and cut its tick population in half by 2028. Ambitious? Certainly. Likely to earn him local plaudits if it’s successful? Absolutely.

There’s mixed news for D.C.’s budget. A new revenue estimate from the city’s chief financial officer finds that D.C. is closing the 2026 fiscal year with $200 million more in revenue than it expected, while also looking at less revenue in the four years to come.

The Kennedy Center was on relatively stable financial footing when Trump took control of the institution, according to internal documents and tax records reviewed byThe Washington Post. Since then, the center has burned through its borrowing capacity, tapped restricted funds and written off $48 million related to unpaid pledges.

The Washington Monument has a new, British neighbor: a time capsule, planted by United States and United Kingdom officials on Tuesday, that won’t be opened until 2276, Justice Covert reports. The capsule, designed by British architect Norman Foster, includes a proclamation from Britain’s King Charles III, signed letters from Trump and Vice President JD Vance, soil from George Washington’s Mount Vernon home and booklets of winning entries from student writing contests.

American University is fostering a new partnership that aims to keep more local public school students in the city, The Sun’s Shamira Muhammad reports. It’s the second D.C. institution to partner with the D.C. College Access Program, which helps public school students use grants and other financial aid to make the cost of attending college low or free. In recent years, AU has admitted more than 40 D.C. students a year, an increase from an earlier average of just 10.





FROM VIRGINIA

Police say a man killed himself after fatally shooting two of his colleagues and wounding a third yesterday morning at the United Rentals facility in Manassas, WTOP reports.





FROM MARYLAND

An essential water use advisory for more than 1.9 million customers in Maryland was lifted Wednesday night. Crews continue to work toward a permanent solution for an electric feed that failed Monday morning at the Washington Suburban Sanitary Commission’s Potomac filtration plant. The facility serves about 70%-75% of WSSC Water’s customers across Montgomery and Prince George’s counties.





TALK TO TOM

Tom Sietsema is back and answering your questions about eating in the D.C. area. Submit your questions here.

How long should restaurants hold tables for late arrivals? 

The general rule is about 15 minutes, sometimes with more flexibility for diners who inform the establishment they are behind schedule.

Ignorance is not bliss. Restaurants like to be informed when someone’s arrival is delayed, because it removes guesswork and helps with planning. Some restaurants have time limits for tables; latecomers may be informed of the fact when they show up. Also, high-end restaurants with tasting menus and multiple seatings might allow for less time, since a latecomer can throw off the pacing of the dinner.

When the tables are turned — when a diner’s reserved table isn’t ready — I think a similar grace period should apply. A thoughtful restaurant might sweeten the wait and throw in a gratis glass of wine or some other small touch to thank a customer for their patience.

For more from Tom, check out this week’s Talk to Tom Q&A.





SPORTS

The Mystics’ season is over after they lost Game 2 of their playoff series against the Atlanta Dream on their home court Wednesday night, The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri reports. Washington, which exceeded expectations this season as the youngest team in the WNBA, has plenty of reason for optimism heading into the offseason, despite the disappointing finish to the year.

Jayden Daniels practiced with the Commanders in London, where the team is preparing for its Week 4 matchup with the Indianapolis Colts. He wore a large brace on his injured left elbow, reports The Sun’s Martenzie Johnson, and it remains unclear if he could return in time for Sunday’s game.

Head coach Dan Quinn said the team will see how Daniels’ elbow, which he dislocated two weeks ago against Dallas, holds up in practice this week before deciding if he’s ready to get back on the field. “We’re not going to put him out there before he’s ready,” Quinn said.





Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@washsun.com.

The newsletter was produced by Matt Berman, Jaden Amos and Erik Schutz.

entries.title: Meet the Capitals’ First-Ever Full-Time Emergency Backup Goalie
entries.summary: The NHL now requires that every team have a full-time, traveling emergency backup goalie. Connor Leslie was up for the challenge.
entries.content:
Capitals goaltending coach Scott Murray keeps a scrupulously maintained directory of local goalies. This part of his job comes up more than you might think: When players need someone in net for their informal summer group skates, or when a guy wants to practice one-timers while team goalies are meant to be resting, Murray is the one to coordinate a substitute. There are some NHL markets flush with options for this kind of arrangement. D.C. is not quite among them.

And so Murray knows every former college goalie in the DMV, anyone who logged a few years in the minor leagues, every local option with enough quality experience to be a serviceable practice goalie for the NHL.

He called on that directory to solve a new problem this summer.

Every NHL team needed to hire an official emergency back-up goalie. Gone are the days of accountants or Zamboni drivers hanging around, ready to pull on gear and occupy the net in case of disaster, like something out of a Disney movie. The NHL’s new collective bargaining agreement requires that every team now have a full-time emergency backup who travels with the team and can functionally serve as an extra practice goalie.

But the new provision comes with some restrictions. Teams cannot use it as a loophole to hire a legitimate third goalie: The new EBUG cannot be someone who has played a single NHL game under a standard player contract. They cannot have appeared in 80 or more professional games at any level, including the minor leagues, and they cannot have played affiliated professional hockey at all in the past three years. In other words, the person must be talented enough to be in net, but not so talented as to have meaningfully pursued a hockey career.

“The parameters weren’t necessarily easy,” Murray said. “Finding a local guy was our goal … But some markets definitely have more goalies hanging around.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

He was able to stay local after all. The Capitals’ first-ever full-time EBUG is 24-year-old Connor Leslie, who grew up in Leesburg, Virginia, where he spent eight years training with the Washington Little Capitals before playing Division III hockey at Amherst College. As a kid with the Little Caps, Leslie practiced at the same facility as the pros.

He now gets to share a rink with them — in a role that is not what he dreamed of as a child, exactly, but a dream all the same.

“It’s pretty surreal,” Leslie said. “I’m over the moon about it.”

When Leslie played his final game at Amherst in 2025, he thought “the only thing I would be doing after that was beer league.” He had no designs on a pro hockey career: Leslie double-majored in political science and psychology and wrote a thesis on terrorists’ digital-recruitment strategies. He eventually hopes to work in federal law enforcement. While looking for a job in the field in the months following graduation, though, he got a call from Murray.

The goaltending coach had long had an entry for Leslie in his local goalie mental Rolodex. But this was not an informal skate over the summer. This was February: It was right after the Olympics, where Capitals starting goalie Logan Thompson had just competed with Team Canada, and Murray wanted to give him the day off. The team needed an extra goalie for a full practice.
Connor_Leslie_093026_0979 copy.jpg (7884x5256, AR: 1.50)Connor_Leslie_093026_0220b.jpg (8192x5464, AR: 1.50)Leslie had not skated in the eight months since he graduated from Amherst, but he felt like he couldn’t possibly say no: “I was just like, You know what? This would be just a really fun opportunity, just to have the story to talk about.” It was. The former D-III goalie pulled himself out of his short retirement and went to the same facility where he logged so many hours as a kid, getting in net for an NHL practice with Alex Ovechkin, Tom Wilson and the other Capitals.

“You’re out there with a bunch of players that you always looked up to,” Leslie said. “I’m looking at Ovechkin out there … It was just one of those moments, where I was like, This can’t be real.”

(That did include taking a one-timer from Ovechkin. “It was one of those where I was just hoping to get my body in front of it by any ways or means possible, even if it was my face,” Leslie said.)

Even after months away from the ice, Leslie felt comfortable. “Honestly, it felt like riding a bike,” he said. “I remembered how much I loved playing … It ended up being a really good skate, surprisingly.”

Murray took note. He had not told Leslie that his invite was for anything other than one day of practice. But the goaltending coach was also scouting for the new EBUG he would have to hire come September. (The new rule was circulating around NHL teams and coaches but had not been made public. Leslie said he had no idea about the changes when he came out for that practice.) Murray liked what he saw from Leslie, who struck him as humble enough to know that he was only there in service to the players, but capable enough for that service to be legitimate.

“They’ve got to be able to stop pucks and challenge guys in whatever situation they’re put in, and then also be able to execute other things that we might need them to be able to do,” Murray said. “I think we’re lucky that we found a guy like Connor.”
Connor_Leslie_093026_0437 copy.jpg (8192x5462, AR: 1.50)Leslie jumped at the opportunity. He will now be the first to define the role with the Caps.

“It’s the first year for every team,” Murray said. “I think it’ll kind of evolve.”

Under the old model, EBUGs generally showed up to the arena for games and waited to see if they would be called on in case of emergency. (They usually were not: A 2025 SportsNet story noted that just six EBUGs had seen the ice in 13,068 regular-season games over the last decade.) It still means being available for that 6-in-13,068 chance, but it will also mean helping with goaltending needs however the organization sees fit, including making it easier for goalies to take a rest day. That’s especially key as the NHL season expands this year to 84 games.

“It just helps us manage the workload,” Capitals goalie Charlie Lindgren said. “I think it’s very beneficial.”

It’s a bigger change for some other NHL teams than it is for the Capitals. The team’s previous emergency goalie, Parker Milner, was more involved with the team than many other franchise EBUGs, and he often helped out at home practices when he could. He’s been chatting with Leslie and is happy to give his blessing to the new kid.

“It instantly struck me that he had the type of personality that could really fit in well,” Milner said. “He had the right mentality … He recognizes that he’s there to help his teammates; he’s not there for himself, and that’s such a big part of it.”

Milner was ineligible to be hired as a full-time EBUG under the new rules. He’d played 245 minor-league games in the ECHL before he became the emergency goalie for the Capitals, which means he had far too much pro experience to qualify. And he was ready to move on to a new life either way. The majority of those ECHL games were played with the Capitals’ affiliate in Charleston, South Carolina, the Stingrays. While playing there, he started building a reputation as a local food writer. He has since moved back to Charleston and become the food and drink editor for The Post and Courier.
Connor_Leslie_093026_1000 copy.jpg (7845x5230, AR: 1.50)The organization saw another benefit in adding Leslie as a regular practice goalie.

Both of the Capitals’ goalies catch with their right hand. (That’s a relatively unusual setup: Of 98 goalies who started an NHL game last season, only five caught right, including Thompson and Lindgren. They became the first pair of right-catching goalies to form an NHL tandem in more than a decade.) Leslie catches with his left hand. That means he can provide an important look in practice for the Capitals.

“Having a guy that catches ‘normal’ can help,” said Lindgren, grinning as he made some heavy air quotes around “normal.” “It’s just the fact of the matter. A right-hand catching goalie is just a different look than a left-hand catching goalie. Not to say that come game time, it’s going to mess our players up, but maybe there’s something in a shootout or a breakaway where it’s more beneficial for them to go and shoot on Les.”

In the meantime, there are other needs he can help fill. Before the start of the season, Capitals medical staff needed to practice their emergency response if a player was severely injured on the ice. Leslie was more than happy to volunteer for the simulation. After all, he figured, he’s here in case of emergency.

entries.title: Morning Sun: They Love Stonks
entries.content:
Today’s notice: Buy low and sell your credibility. Gillibrand helps Nixon in Florida. A Democrat leads yet another poll in Kansas. A deep dive into Michigan’s 7th. Chuck Schumer, speechless. And: You can buy a skateboard from Tim Burchett as long as he doesn’t sell it to you. 





THE LATEST

The most consequential miss of this Congress? Stock trading on the Hill is alive and well after a proposed ban failed to advance yesterday along party lines. Our team reported out the spin from the vote’s defeat, and it’s as you’d expect — Republicans say it was Democrats’ fault, Democrats say it was Republicans who blew it. You could probably have made a bet on that in a prediction market. But this one may really leave a mark.

The sleeper issue of this election cycle is the public anger over members of Congress trading. The Washington Sun’s Paul Kane and Avani Kalra write that both parties are trying to take advantage, and both are telling the same story: that lawmakers are using inside information to buy and sell stocks to get rich. Should work out great for Congress’ approval rating next year.

Congress hasn’t acted on this because not enough members think it’s a good idea to. The Sun’s Dave Levinthal — the dean of the congressional stock trade press corps — wrote a detailed postmortem to yesterday’s vote that tracks the resistance to legislative action from top Democrats and Republicans. Dave describes how members actually made their perception problem worse by repeatedly demonstrating how comically rickety the STOCK Act is — you know, the transparency law that was supposed to help the public understand that members are not insider traders.

Republican and Democratic lawmakers have violated the act’s disclosure provisions on a nearly 1-to-1 basis this decade, Dave writes.

Back to the campaign trail: Everyone is now promising voters that they will take action on congressional stock trading. But here’s the secret: everyone also rolls their eyes at this voter outrage. Most lawmakers dismiss the idea that they are sitting behind their desks on Capitol Hill getting tips and buying and selling stocks, Paul and Avani report. They are taking little action to disprove it, however. That cognitive dissonance could ring out for a long time.

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


Scoop: DSCC chair boosts Angie Nixon in Florida. The surprise progressive Democratic nominee in the long-shot Florida race will get some help from Washington today. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand (D-New York), the chair of Senate Democrats’ fundraising arm, will host a virtual event for Nixon, a source familiar with the plans told The Sun’s Stephen Neukam. Nixon said this week that the DSCC has not committed to helping her air ads.

First on The Sun: More good news for Democrats in Kansas? There are signs of momentum for Democrat Chris Mann in his race for attorney general against Republican incumbent Kris Kobach, according to a new poll by the Democratic Attorneys General Association shared first with The Sun. Mann leads the poll 47% to 46% on the strength of support from registered independents (56% to 29%) and Kobach’s high negatives (48% unfaves). DAGA was early to target Kansas for a flip, and the new numbers reflect some movement toward Democrats since a survey taken by the group last November, which found Kobach up 46% to 44%.

More: Trump Announces $54B Investment in a State With Tight Senate Race

FROM MICHIGAN


Rep. Tom Barrett walks the tightrope: The Sun’s Elena Schneider reports from Lansing, where the Republican incumbent is in Advanced Placement campaign mode. He needs to win over frustrated independents who are fleeing from Republicans, according to public and private polling, while energizing a deflated GOP base. In short, he needs to make the race all about his opponent, progressive Democratic nominee William Lawrence, while also making it just enough about himself, too.

Two quotes that define this race:

From Barrett, who crossed Donald Trump on the Iran war and drew criticism from the president — but needs voters who love the president to turn out for him in big numbers: “I think that we are a party that can handle, you know, differences of opinion.”

From Lawrence, who is trying to bat away the years of social media baggage that has been a big part of the messaging against him: “People understand that anything that one says on Twitter, as a private citizen, is to be taken with a heavy dash of salt.”

FROM THE HILL


Department of Ready to GTFO: Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer held a presser yesterday ahead of senators jetting out of town for the sprint to Election Day. The Sun’s Igor Bobic noted that the event lasted a whole five minutes. Democrats have “the wind in our sails,” Schumer told reporters. He ignored a question about the future of party leadership, and that was the end of that. More on those jet fumes from The Sun’s Al Weaver.

NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

It’s hard to sell skateboards in Congress, and not just because your average member is old and out of shape. The Sun’s Emily Kennard sings the ballad of Rep. Tim Burchett’s nascent homemade board business, a tale of trying unsuccessfully to navigate Byzantine congressional ethics rules. The Tennessee Republican can’t put his name on his boards or associate himself with them directly.

“I get it. I get it,” Burchett told Emily. “You know, somebody wants to sway my vote, and they come buy a skateboard from me, or something.”

Burchett finds the whole thing laughable, given what we opened this newsletter with. “I’m not trying to do any insider stock trading. I’m just trying to sell a few skateboards,” he said.

entries.title: How One Republican Plans to Survive a Blue Wave
entries.summary: “I've kind of carved a little bit of an identity,” Rep. Tom Barrett said. Republicans know he’ll need luck, too.
entries.content:
LANSING, Michigan — Republican Rep. Tom Barrett toasted to good luck last Saturday, as the guest of honor at the Hmong New Year Festival at a local park.

He’s already gotten some this year. This fall, he’ll just need a lot more.

The freshman congressman is hoping to join an ever-shrinking club of incumbents in battleground districts who can hold off midterm challengers fueled by voters’ anger at the party in power. Barrett, who was one of the first Republicans to vote against President Donald Trump’s war in Iran, is attempting to build his own brand without losing GOP base support, even as public polling has found Democrats holding a 10-point advantage on the generic ballot in Michigan.

“I've kind of carved a little bit of an identity,” Barrett said in an interview during a car ride between campaign events last weekend, referring to his Iran war votes.

Still, he knows what he’s up against. “It’s no secret that the political environment today is not what it was in 2024,” when he won by just under 4 percentage points, while Trump won the district by more than 1 point. Trump’s approval rating now hovers at 36% in Michigan.

“Sure, wave elections happen,” he added. “I guess we'll find out in 38 days, won't we?”

Barrett is pursuing a tightrope strategy that few House candidates can pull off in a hyper-partisan environment, particularly after mid-decade redistricting wiped out more swing seats over the past year. He has to win over frustrated independents who are fleeing from Republicans, according to public and private polling, while energizing a deflated GOP base. And he’s already gotten an unexpected boost from a Democratic opponent with unique vulnerabilities.

He explained his path to victory as a two-track playbook. “It is going out and telling the story of what I've done that may be a little bit unconventional,” he said. “The other is the radical way that my opponent has carried himself for the last 15 years, and that contrast.”

He has allies in his approach. In September, Republican Reps. Mariannette Miller-Meeks and Zach Nunn of Iowa, running in hotly contested races, joined Barrett in voting against Trump’s Iran war powers. Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick of Pennsylvania has also voted against the war since June. All four have also tried to tag their Democratic opponents as socialists and extremists in TV ads.

“The way you should deal, as an incumbent Republican, with a wave is to find some distance between yourself and the party brand, and then you go after your opponent,” said former GOP Rep. Charlie Dent, who represented a competitive Pennsylvania district and survived the 2006 midterms. “In this environment, I think you need multiple points of separation.”

Barrett hasn’t completely distanced himself from the president. When Trump campaigned in Barrett’s district in July, Barrett appeared alongside him. He attended the president’s Rose Garden dinner with other battleground House Republicans in September, but he didn’t join the party’s midterm convention in Dallas.

When asked about Democrats’ attacks on his ties to the president, Barrett said it’s “no secret to anybody” that he’s a Republican who voted for Trump. “I think that we are a party that can handle, you know, differences of opinion,” he said.

In June, Trump called the four Republicans who voted to limit military action in Iran “bad Republicans” and “unpatriotic” in a Truth Social post. At the time, Barrett said, Trump’s White House “team was very, very vocal” about his vote. Barrett said he met with the White House Counsel’s office, which argued “it wasn't war in the sense that the Constitution prescribes,” but Barrett remained unmoved.

“I had a number of conversations afterward with members who told me they agreed with or really respected my vote, but didn't feel like they could vote that way,” Barrett said. “They were worried about, I think, political factors.”

Those factors are different today with gas averaging $4.43 a gallon. “It sounds convenient now, however many months later, with the war in Iran being such an unpopular thing, but that was not the frame of mind that I was looking at," he added.

For Barrett, a 22-year Army veteran who served in Afghanistan and Guantánamo Bay, the “devastating effects of the war on terror and war” has “really shaped my opinion on this.” Barrett described another particularly personal vote in 2025 to repeal congressional authorization for the war in Iraq, in which he served alongside Rep. John James, Michigan’s Republican gubernatorial candidate, though they didn’t know each other at the time.

Barrett said James asked him on the House floor, “‘Did you ever think we'd vote to end the war we were deployed in?’ I'm like, ‘No, I didn't,’” he recounted. “Unfortunately, it's become too easy to get into war and far too hard to get out of it.”

His votes on Iran have benefited him in reaching angry voters. Barrett said his opposition to the war has opened “a crack in the door to have that conversation” with voters who are furious about rising gas prices, so it’s “given me a little bit of a conversation point to talk about this, where they may not have otherwise been open to that discussion.”

But it’s not clear whether voters will differentiate Barrett from Trump in November. “That’s the big question of the cycle,” said Robert Blizzard, a top Republican pollster who is not working on this race. “But the party and Trump are so synonymous that they may not be able to do it.”

A disciplined strategy only goes so far in a wave. As one national Republican consultant said: “How do incumbents survive in a tough environment? It’s better to be lucky than good.”

Republicans believe Barrett caught that lucky break in August, when William Lawrence emerged from a three-way primary to win the Democratic nomination in the district. Lawrence, a co-founder of the climate activism group Sunrise Movement, beat two centrist candidates who divided the center-left lane. Lawrence won through a strong ground game and endorsements from national lawmakers, including Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders.

Lawrence comes with baggage, as Democrats privately admit. He has deleted hundreds of social media posts, as first reported by CNN, that called for defunding the police and criticized the nuclear family structure, calling it a “violent way of organizing society.” Lawrence was a member of the Democratic Socialists of America, but he recently let his membership lapse.

In an interview after a meet-and-greet in Okemos, Michigan, that drew more than 50 people, Lawrence said that “there's “things I said in the past that I've changed my mind, there's things I've said that I didn't even agree with at the time. I was just, you know, angry, blowing off steam.”

Lawrence said he no longer stands by his call to defund the police. He believes voters, especially millennials and Gen Zers, understand that people are just "thinking out loud on the internet.”

“That's where all kinds of random, off-the-dome thoughts go, especially in those pandemic years,” he said. “People understand that anything that one says on Twitter, as a private citizen, is to be taken with a heavy dash of salt.”

Some Democrats believe Lawrence was “the weakest candidate” of the three who ran in the primary, said a Michigan Democratic lawmaker, also granted anonymity to speak candidly. They wondered if Lawrence would be able to “hold on to this seat,” should he win it this year, “in 2028,” a potentially more difficult environment for Democrats.

A national Democratic strategist, also granted anonymity to discuss the issue candidly, called Lawrence’s social media posts “not helpful.”

“Does his candidacy make it a tougher lift and require more money that could’ve been used elsewhere? Yes,” the strategist said. “But will we win it? Yes.”

Lawrence’s vulnerabilities are compounded by the Michigan Senate race, where Abdul El-Sayed also beat the more moderate candidate. Many Republicans believe the pair offer a one-two punch against an “extreme strain of radical ideology,” Barrett said.

Much of the $18 million in Republican-backed spending has cast Lawrence as a “socialist” who wants to “dismantle America.”

The national GOP consultant described this line of attack as essential. “You motivate Republicans through fear and the fact that these crazies could get elected,” they said. “If you're an incumbent, getting Democrats underwater quickly is very important, then keeping them there.”

“Lawrence is nuts, and Tom is not,” said Jamie Roe, a Michigan-based Republican consultant. “The people of that district, maybe outside the university, are not that far left. Tom is very much more in tune with where the voters are at, compared to Lawrence.”

That line of attack could resonate with people like Tim Stuck, a 53-year-old attending a Michigan State University tailgate, where Barrett greeted potential voters Saturday afternoon. While Barrett worked the crowd and grabbed bites of a cheeseburger, Stuck described himself as an independent, undecided voter who was frustrated by the economy and high gas prices.

He said he has been “open” to voting for a Democrat, but he’s unsure about Lawrence’s more progressive ideas, because “I’m more of a traditional person.”

“He’s not a cookie-cutter Republican,” Sean Bertolino, a Republican voter from Williamston said of Barrett after greeting him at an MSU tailgate. “This might be a bad year [for Republicans], and so if you had someone running against Tom who's a lot more reasonable, and not, frankly, crazy, then I don’t know.”

Democrats, despite their reservations, believe the political environment will carry Lawrence over the finish line. And Lawrence argued that a progressive can flip a battleground seat because “our politics is as much about top-versus-bottom as it is against left-versus-right, and I'm out there every day among the people, working alongside people.”

“Tom Barrett is nowhere to be found and is voting with his president Donald Trump every single time,” he said, “Every single time it's mattered, he's been there, and the consequences are measured in higher prices and the decline of our rule of law and global humiliation for the United States.”

entries.title: Senate Republicans Leave Town Wondering: Did We Do Enough?
entries.summary: “I hate to leave good bills on the table, but I understand that some of my colleagues want to get back and start campaigning again,” Sen. John Kennedy said.
entries.content:
Republicans made a last-gasp bid Wednesday to answer simmering anger in the electorate, holding a pair of failed show votes on high costs and corruption, then recessing until after the midterms.

Republican leaders had considered leaving sooner so members could campaign, as the House did, but stuck around after GOP senators clamored for votes on items they could use in those campaigns.

It was partially successful. After spending more than a week passing a package to overhaul college sports — which may or may not die in the House — they had to settle for failed procedural votes on a bill aimed at curbing energy costs from data centers and another to curtail stock trading by lawmakers. Democrats derided both as toothless.

The closing record left some lawmakers worried the moves were too little, too late with less than five weeks until Election Day, especially as the Iran war drags on and gas prices remain near highs for the year.

“You’re always concerned that if you could do more, you should do more,” said Sen. Mike Rounds (R-South Dakota). “We know the American people are hurting right now. We know that.”

“I think the current status right now with prices being high on petroleum products in particular … it hurts anybody who’s currently in office,” Rounds said. “If the price of gas were to go down by a dollar a gallon right now, that would really help.”

The party in power has found itself on the backfoot on a number of fronts as voters prepare to cast ballots. President Donald Trump’s approval rating has cratered nationally, weighing on incumbents and candidates in key battleground states.

On top of gas prices, Republicans are dealing with record-high diesel prices and the ramifications of Trump’s decision to remove tariffs on imported beef, especially in the Midwest where farmers have been hit hard.

The grim electoral outlook prompted Republican leaders to hold those last-minute votes, including the vote on the data center bill designed to boost its sponsor, embattled Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio).

Husted has been pilloried back home for his past support for data centers when he was Ohio’s lieutenant governor and appeared at numerous ribbon cuttings for them. Former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown’s campaign has dubbed him “the face of data centers.”

“I think it’s an important message to send. That we are listening and we understand people’s concerns about data centers raising their electricity rates, and are determined to make sure that doesn’t happen,” Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas) said. “I think it’s an important message, pretty much everywhere.”

“The election’s still a month off,” Cornyn added, arguing “it’s not too late to spread that message.”

Democrats, however, were not in the mood to hand Republicans an electoral boost and blocked the bill. Only four — Sens. Maggie Hassan of New Hampshire, Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota, Jon Ossoff of Georgia and Raphael Warnock of Georgia — voted to advance Husted’s proposal.

The minority party also blocked a Republican measure aimed at curbing stock trading among members of Congress. The issue has become a frequent topic in campaign ads.

Although Republicans were pleased they squeezed the votes in under the wire, there is concern that the party controlling the White House and Capitol Hill has not done enough since the start of the Iran war to bring down costs.

Lawmakers have tried to pitch what they consider to be popular parts of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to voters, only to see the war overshadow their sales job. Even Lara Trump, the president’s daughter-in-law, conceded conflict could be costly at the polls.

Some had pushed for Senate Majority Leader John Thune to seek some wins prior to the August recess with a third reconciliation bill, which would have used expedited budget rules to pass bills on a simple majority. But the party was unable to find the requisite 51 votes needed to plow ahead.

Some members worried they spent much of the September passing a bill overhauling college sports rather than working on affordability concerns.

“I hate to leave good bills on the table, but I understand that some of my colleagues want to get back and start campaigning again,” said Sen. John Kennedy (R-Louisiana), who has complained the Senate used its dwindling time to make “the football coaches happy.”

“We should have started right after we passed [OBBBA]. We’re leaving two reconciliation efforts on the table,” Kennedy said. “You can say, ‘Well we’ll do it in the lame duck,’ but you don’t know what people’s moods are going to be.”

Kennedy also lamented that the chamber has not voted on a pair of Congressional Review Act resolutions, including one to nix energy regulations that could result in lower costs.

“It is legislative malpractice if the United States Senate is not allowed this week to vote to kill these rules,” he said in a floor speech Tuesday.

The party has also struggled to respond to stubbornly high gas and diesel prices that are causing major consternation for Republicans in farm states, especially as polling numbers have dipped considerably.

The idea of a diesel export ban has been bandied about, but members were torn over choosing the right path forward. Thune told reporters that Trump has yet to make a final decision on that front.

The leader also cautioned that even if they did make a move, it may not matter with so little time before voters make up their minds.

“I think we’ve done everything we can do,” said Sen. Kevin Cramer (R-North Dakota). “Whether or not it’s enough, I guess we’ll see in the numbers.”

entries.title: A Lawmaker Wants His Longboard Sales to Be Aboveboard
entries.summary: Rep. Tim Burchett has found trying to sell his handmade skateboards frustrating, given Congress’ typically toothless ethics rules.
entries.content:
When Rep. Tim Burchett is in his Tennessee district, he spends hours a week in his barn — usually between 10 p.m. and 4 a.m. — handcrafting longboards. He often jokes that the niche hobby is “cheaper than a psychiatrist.”

It turns out he might have to consult one from the sheer stress it’s causing him. He’s spent considerable time trying unsuccessfully to figure out how to sell the boards in a way that complies with congressional ethics rules. It’s become a grating journey for him, given that Congress’ notoriously toothless ethics rules are still holding him back.

“It's just taking a lot of time, and it’s costing me a lot of money to do the right thing,” Burchett told The Washington Sun. “I’m incredibly frustrated.”

“Maybe I won't ever be able to sell them.”

The Republican occasionally causes problems in his conference. He’s developed a habit of changing his mind about major bills at the last minute, something he considers part of his legislative strategy. It’s almost as if he enjoys being whipped by leadership for his vote. As a fiscal hawk, he frequently aligns with the House Freedom Caucus, though he’s not a member because he says he doesn’t like caucuses.

When it comes to his skateboards — which gained attention after Tulsi Gabbard, his former House colleague and the former Director of National Intelligence, posted about the one he gave her — he’s trying to play by the book.

Burchett’s latest proposal to the House Ethics Committee is for his wife to set up a business that could sell them. Then, Pluto Sports, a local skate shop in Knoxville, could buy and resell the boards — so long as they don't advertise them with the lawmaker’s name or likeness, according to House Ethics rules.

“Basically, I'm just gonna be the guy in the shop,” Burchett explained.

Outside the saws and sanders, the rest of the skateboard business would have to be out of his hands. He doesn’t know what a brand might be called, but he knows he wouldn’t be allowed to promote its products.

It's unclear whether this proposal will be approved. Tom Rust, the chief counsel for the House Ethics Committee, declined to comment when The Sun asked about it.

“I'm just trying to do everything right and legal, and I just — you know, it's funny. Some of these guys in Congress have said I should’ve just done it and not told them about it,” Burchett said.

The main hurdle is complying with the House Ethics manual, which says: “At times a Member or staff person wishes to engage in outside employment that involves the selling of goods or services. On the basis of the rules and standards of conduct set out above, a Member should not undertake any outside employment that would involve the Member personally in the selling or endorsement of any goods or services.”

It's especially irritating for Burchett when he compares his financial ambitions to those of his colleagues: This Congress, he’s pushed to restrict lawmakers’ ability to trade stocks — a practice that’s proved wildly profitable for many members, but has also remained wildly unpopular among Americans for years now.

“I'm not trying to do any insider stock trading. I'm just trying to sell a few skateboards,” Burchett said.

Lawmakers being able to trade stocks while serving in Congress is a big reason that Burchett holds open contempt for politics-as-usual in Washington, which he calls a “sewer.”

He thinks what he’s been trying to do is much different, though he says he understands why the ethics rules prohibiting him from starting a business are in place.

“I get it. I get it,” he said. “You know, somebody wants to sway my vote, and they come buy a skateboard from me, or something.”

Burchett can’t talk up his own boards too much, but others can vouch for his work: Brian Beauchene, a longtime skateboarder, the owner of Pluto Sports and a hometown friend of Burchett’s, said “they are real good quality” longboards for casual skateboarders.

He stopped short of commending Burchett’s skating skills, going only so far as to say, “He's competent.”

“I try not to get involved in too much politics, myself. But when it comes to skateboarding, I'm all about it, and if he's going to make some skateboards, well, I'm going to help him put good trucks and wheels on,” Beauchene said. “I'm happy that he's doing it. It brings some good attention to skateboarding that, you know, even politicians can ride skateboards.”

In the meantime, Burchett’s colleagues can continue trading stocks.

On Wednesday, the Stop Insider Trading Act died in the Senate. The bill, which the House passed in July, would have prohibited members, their spouses and children from buying new stocks, while allowing members to keep existing stocks.

Burchett said the bill didn't go far enough compared to other stock-ban efforts he’s supported this Congress, but it was “better than nothing.”

“My bill was just a total ban on it. Just put all your money in a mutual fund. You make sacrifices when you're in Congress,” Burchett said.

Danielle Caputo, senior legal counsel with Campaign Legal Center, said Burchett’s proposed business structure sounds like a “low-level concern for improper influence,” as long as “they’re not specifically being sold as like, ‘Representative Burchett’s skateboards.’”

Burchett said he’s trying to do the right thing, but what could have happened if he followed his unnamed colleagues’ advice and didn’t bother to seek guidance or approval from the Ethics Committee beforehand?

“It would probably, at that point, just be like a letter of admonishment or something like that, and telling him that he has to stop selling his skateboards,” Caputo said. “The House Ethics Committee does not have a great record of doing anything meaningful, and I don't imagine that they would find this to be that serious of a violation.”

Still, he wants the process to be aboveboard, and everyone seems to be asking the 62-year-old where they can get his skateboards.

“I just don't have a lot of time to, as much as I'd hope to, to satisfy all those people,” he said. “I have people, weekly, calling, people wanting to buy 'em from me, that wanna get one for their grandkid or something. And then charities, of course, are calling, too. And it’s just, I don’t know what direction to go in, actually.”

He repeatedly asserted that setting up shop has been so difficult in part because he’s made too many enemies in the chamber.

“I've ruffled a lot of feathers since I've been in Congress," he said. "So I totally expected this.”

entries.title: Stock Trading Emerges as a Brutal Weapon for Both Parties
entries.summary: The perception of insider trading has prompted a wave of attack ads, and a last-ditch Senate vote.
entries.content:
WILLIAMSBURG, Va. — Sometimes back-to-back, usually within the same two-minute window of advertising, voters here get treated to the same type of brutal attack ad, from both parties.

Republicans are running ads attacking former congresswoman Elaine Luria over stock trades she made during her two terms in the House, saying “something is fishy” about the Democrat’s wealth. They often roll right into an ad from Democrats bashing Republican Rep. Rob Wittman in the neighboring southeast Virginia district for trading stocks in companies he “may have had confidential information about.”

It’s become the sleeper issue of the election cycle, with accusations flying from both parties that lawmakers are using inside information to buy and sell stocks to pad their personal wealth. So much so that Senate Republicans, with some of their own facing similar lines of attack, rushed a vote Wednesday on legislation that would ban stock trades by members of Congress.

Republican leaders knew that the legislation was not fully baked and did not have nearly enough support, so they tacked on some conservative election law provisions that ensured Democrats would oppose the bill.

The final vote tally — all 53 Republicans voting yes, while all 47 members of the Democratic caucus voted to block the measure — came as expected. Out on the campaign trail, Republicans now hope to blame Democrats for allowing members to trade stocks, an issue that started to percolate about five years ago but now has hit a full boil with the voting public.

“Americans have a low opinion of us as members of Congress, whether the House or the Senate, especially in keeping the inside information we have separate from our financials,” Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts, whose family wealth is in the hundreds of millions of dollars, told The Washington Sun. “This bill is designed to restore that faith.”

Ricketts is facing an unusually strong reelection challenge in Nebraska. Independent Dan Osborn has repeatedly accused Ricketts of making millions in the stock market while serving in Congress, a recurring theme the challenger hit on during a debate in early September.

Senate Majority Leader John Thune previewed Republicans’ line of attack on Tuesday when asked if the vote could make the difference for Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska), a vulnerable incumbent who has been attacked by his Democratic opponent, former Rep. Mary Peltola, for being one of the most prolific stock traders in Congress.

“It makes it pretty hard for Democrats to make that argument,” Thune said of Democrats’ campaign messaging on stock trading, though he also pointed to failed data center legislation. “These are both, as I said, broadly bipartisan bills that have passed the House with huge majorities, all of which get at the issues that the Democrats seem to find able to use in their campaigns.”

Thirteen Democrats voted for the stock bill in the House.

Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) slammed Republicans for including voter identification provisions in the bill, saying that it was designed as a political ploy. But Schatz told The Sun he is not worried about the potential ramifications of the vote.

“There are no votes on the way out of town that are going to shift public opinion,” Schatz said of Republicans’ moves. “I'm not very worried that suddenly people are going to think that prices are coming down, or that they've been focused on regular people all this time because they've done a couple of moves to try to get it right.”

Ricketts batted down accusations that those voter provisions were specifically included for political reasons. He added that he would be willing to work with Democratic leadership on a new version of the bill –– but only after November.

“Thirty-six states have streamlined voter ID, including many blue states,” Ricketts said. “But I’ll certainly work with leadership with regard to where to go from here if this vote fails.”

The stock bill was one of several votes Republicans held this week that had a sharp political message behind them, including one designed to help local governments deal with energy prices from data centers. It also got blocked by Democrats.

In House and Senate races across the nation, accusations of corruption have been a focal point in campaign ads. But the issue of individual lawmakers trading stocks has become particularly potent, according to campaign operatives in both parties.

A 2012 law requires lawmakers to reveal, in a timely manner, purchases or sales that they make in publicly traded stocks, in addition to a broad financial disclosure form they must file on an annual basis that includes data such as real estate holdings and spousal income.

Since just last summer almost 40 members of the House and Senate have violated the timing requirements of that law, filing their disclosure forms on stock trades later than the mandate, according to a review by The Sun.

These filings have proven to be great fodder for opposition researchers in both parties.

In New Jersey, Republican Rep. Tom Kean Jr. took several months off the daily work of Congress and went into in-patient therapy for depression. Yet Kean’s financial adviser continued to make stock trades for the congressman even while he was not able to work, drawing charges of being “one of [the] most prolific traders” in Congress in a debate this week.

In northeast Pennsylvania, Democrats have pummeled first-term Rep. Rob Bresnahan (R-Pennsylvania) for campaigning two years ago on the “sickening” idea that lawmakers would make big money, only to then turn into a prolific stock trader himself. According to a Sun analysis, he made 650 trades last year, before The Sun tracked how that volume decreased as he entered the election season.

Most lawmakers feel that these charges are grossly exaggerated and that they use financial advisers to handle their investments, dismissing the idea that they are sitting behind their desks on Capitol Hill getting tips and buying and selling stocks.

Many lawmakers start blind trusts or place all their financial holdings into mutual funds or other investment devices that don’t involve direct buying and selling.

But those defenses sometimes get dismissed by an angry public that despises Congress, giving political operatives a chance to pick and choose the timing of these sales to raise questions about a lawmaker’s ethics.

Any trades happening right around the time of a big congressional vote can get turned into a very potent ad.

Dozens of these ads are running across the nation, but the Norfolk, Virginia, media market might represent political ground zero for the barrage of stock-trading ads, as each party looks to use the issue in two critical battlegrounds that could determine the House majority.

“Rob Wittman has only served himself,” a retired U.S. Marshal says in an ad run by the House Majority PAC, a super PAC aligned with Democratic leaders.

An image on the screen says the 19-year incumbent Republican’s personal wealth is “now worth up to $7.6 million,” accusing him of supporting policies that raised prices on everyday Virginians.

Wittman also says that a financial adviser handles his stock trading. He posted on his campaign website a section explaining that, while he has made lots of trades, he hasn’t made much money.

“Trading volume is not income. Trading volume is not profit. And trading volume is not an increase in net worth,” Wittman said.

Republicans have returned the favor in accusing Luria, trying to knock off Rep. Jen Kiggans (R-Virginia) in a rematch of their 2022 race, of making “millions” in her two terms from 2019 to 2023.

“Elaine Luria votes for massive chip subsidy legislation, holds millions in chip stocks,” the screen on the ad reads.

Another ad accused her of making $21 million in stock trades while in office, an accusation that local TV news refuted in a fact-check segment. Still, Luria’s net wealth when she left Congress was between $3.4 million and $12.9 million.

The House passed its stock-trading ban back in the summer, but most Democrats opposed the ban as toothless for not imposing the same restrictions on the president and Cabinet members.

Some lawmakers who have worked on this issue, especially those not up for reelection this year, feel that politics are driving how party leaders handle the matter, preventing them from working toward a solution that would help improve Congress’ image.

“This is one of those measures that everybody says they are for, and run on in their campaigns, Democrats and Republicans, but when it comes time to vote for it, they don’t want to,” Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Missouri), the author of another stock-trading proposal, told The Sun.
