entries.title: Talk to Tom: A Legendary French Spot in Great Falls Gets New Owners
entries.summary: Plus: An ideal pre-theater spot on 14th street, where to eat in Charleston, and how long restaurants should hold tables for late arrivals.
entries.content:
Welcome to Talk to Tom, the dining-advice column that aims to point you toward good meals, steer you from the dross and solve your pressing restaurant queries. Look for a fresh Q&A every Thursday in this space.

Questions and comments can be submitted to TalkToTom@washingtonsun.com. Submissions may be edited for length and clarity.

We are dying to know what your opinion is of Thompson Restaurants taking over L’Auberge Chez François, the local institution known for its impressive fine dining and impeccable service in Great Falls.

It was time for a change, says Jacques Haeringer, who turns 77 next month and has been with the family-run dining destination since 1976. While he says L’Auberge Chez Francois had its “best year ever last year,” he welcomed the idea of a restaurant company with deep pockets taking over the production, which employs almost 100 staff members and includes the more relaxed Jacques’ Brasserie downstairs. Just as important, the veteran chef says owner Warren Thompson, whose dining portfolio is largely casual and mid-market, is committed to keeping the Alsatian menu and the ambiance that generations of customers have come to expect. The deal, finalized in late August, keeps Haeringer on as a consultant to maintain standards.

Yours truly trusts but also verifies, so I booked dinner at L’Auberge Chez Francois this past Sunday. It was encouraging to see a full parking lot, then to be led to a timbered dining room, where servers in familiar red vests zoomed over with a flurry of menus, and other staff dropped off the restaurant’s signature garlic toast and herbed cottage cheese along with bread and butter. The script was the same as on my last visit five years ago, with selections including a mushroom-filled chive crepe and rack of lamb, and a set price dinner menu with multiple courses: amuse bouche, starter, salad, palate-cleansing sorbet, entree, and dessert. (You want to come hungry.) The hearty portions remind you you’re eating in the suburbs, while the stocks, sauces, and turned vegetables — some plucked from the restaurant’s garden outside — reflect classical French training.
L’Auberge_Chez François_093026_0188 copy.jpg (7759x5173, AR: 1.50)The stars of the night were a demitasse of corn chowder, plump sweetbreads and earthy mushrooms with Madeira sauce, a punchy Caesar salad, a textbook perfect Dover sole sweetened with sautéed lobster, and a choucroute — rich with foie gras, sausage slices, and tangy sauerkraut — that’s worth the drive from D.C. (Let me add that the light, billowy Grand Marnier soufflé garnished with strips of candied orange was actually superior to my last one here.) And Haeringer, dressed in his chef whites and cracking his usual dad jokes for an appreciative audience, made an appearance in the honey-lit dining room. “Mr. Thompson moved into the neighborhood,” I overheard the chef tell a table of customers, no doubt to ease worries about the change.

A gallery in the basement hallway pays homage to a restaurant that originally opened as Chez Francois in Washington in 1954. Jacques Haeringer’s father, chef François Haeringer, relocated to Great Falls the year of the country’s bicentennial and remained a presence in the kitchen until his death at 91, in 2010.
L’Auberge_Chez François_093026_0044b.jpg (7687x5125, AR: 1.50)L’Auberge_Chez François_093026_0399b.jpg (6830x4554, AR: 1.50)You can see, then, why regulars might be concerned. Not to worry, says Ruben Paredes, managing director of Thompson Restaurants, who’s in charge of the transition. “Our big mission is not to change anything that makes L’Auberge Chez Francois an institution,” he says. “We have no intention of changing the food, service or ambience.” The acquisition is focused mainly on behind-the-scenes improvements, including purchasing power and technology, Paredes says. By way of example, the new owner is adding Starlink to improve -internet connections in the semirural area.

Haeringer jokes that there’s just one infrastructure detail to which the new steward of the institution isn’t committed: “They won’t be paying for my facelift.”

It is good to have you back! I am writing to ask for restaurant recommendations in Charleston, South Carolina. We have no price-point restrictions — anything from neighborhood spots to fine dining would do — and are open to any cuisine.

Count me a big fan of Charleston, which I ranked as one of America’s Top 10 food cities (in 2015, a designation that still holds). Some of my favorite restaurants back then — Fig, Leon’s Fine Poultry & Oysters and The Obstinate Daughter — are still around and still choice.

My go-to food guide in Charleston is Parker Milner, the food editor of The Post and Courier, to whom I put your question for a current take. He served up three recommendations:

“Chez Nous, which opened 12 years ago and comes from the owners of Michelin-starred Malagón, serves a daily changing offering, with two appetizers, two entrees and two desserts handwritten on paper menus in chef-owner Jill Mathias’ stylish script. The intriguing, invigorating food is reminiscent of what I’ve had in Paris with a Lowcountry twist.

Merci, a 24-seat spot in the Harleston Village neighborhood, is serving some of the most inspired plates in Charleston right now. Chef Michael Zentner (you may recognize the name from his days in D.C., when he cooked at Alta Strada) offers excellent house-made breads, produce-driven small plates, and entrees that range from the celebratory beef Wellington to poulet pressé with moutarde violette.

Lastly, The Restaurant at Zero George is my top fine-dining pick right now. Chef Vinson Petrillo works tirelessly to excite diners through a mix of innovative bites (edible ‘cigars’ with beef tartare and brown butter ‘ash,’ for instance) and premium ingredients. His tasting menu is served in a historic boutique hotel in the heart of the Charleston peninsula.”

How long should restaurants hold tables for late arrivals?

The general rule is about 15 minutes, sometimes with more flexibility for diners who inform the establishment they are behind schedule.

Ignorance is not bliss. Restaurants like to be informed when someone’s arrival is delayed, because it removes guesswork and helps with planning. Some restaurants have time limits for tables; latecomers may be informed of the fact when they show up. Also, high-end restaurants with tasting menus and multiple seatings might allow for less time, since a latecomer can throw off the pacing of the dinner.

When the tables are turned — when a diner’s reserved table isn’t ready — I think a similar grace period should apply. A thoughtful restaurant might sweeten the wait and throw in a gratis glass of wine or some small touch to thank a customer for their patience.

I’ll be going to Studio Theater soon. What’s quick and easy nearby?

How about quick, easy, delicious — and right across the street? Katsumi is all those things and more. The Japanese restaurant on 14th St. NW recently impressed me not just with the cooking, but with its hospitality. No sooner did I sit down on a plush seat than an attendant let me know I arrived in time to order from the happy hour menu, which is offered from 5 p.m. to 7 p.m. daily and includes a couple of juicy grilled chicken skewers for $6, or half the regular cost. When a companion needed a moment to review the drinks list, the server said, “No rush. You’re the boss tonight,” as if we were the only customers on a busy Saturday.

Then the dishes from Masaaki “Uchi” Uchino started landing: a tuna roll, drizzled with spicy pink mayonnaise and ignited with wasabi seaweed. Fatty tuna nigiri that laid buttery, melt-on-the-tongue raw fish on a pad of well-seasoned rice. A crunchy heap of hot fried chicken kissed with honey miso. Katsumi is an ideal preshow spot, offering food that leaves you sated but won’t put you to sleep by the second act.

The signature drinks show skill, too. Some like it hot. For them, there’s Daimo Verde — tequila swirled with Alpine liqueur and a shishito cordial, among other enhancers, presented with a rectangle of ice and a ribbon of cucumber in a long glass.

entries.title: Renee Good's Family Sues Immigration Officials Over Her Killing in Minneapolis
entries.summary: One lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights.
entries.content:
By Kathy Mccormack and Mark Vancleave

MINNEAPOLIS — Renee Good’s family sued the U.S. government and several immigration officials Thursday, alleging wrongful death, conspiracy and other violations in the 37-year-old woman’s killing by an immigration officer during a federal crackdown in Minneapolis.

The two lawsuits were filed by Good’s partner, Becca Good, and Renee's brother Brent Ganger.

The Justice Department didn’t immediately respond to an email seeking comment on the lawsuits.

Renee Good, a mother of three, was fatally shot Jan. 7 as protests against immigration raids flared across the city. According to Becca Good, her partner stopped their car in a street to support neighbors during an immigration operation.

Bystander video shows Renee Good in the driver’s seat of a red SUV blocking part of the road and repeatedly honking her horn.

Two immigration officers get out of a truck, their faces covered, and one orders Good to get out of the car. She reverses briefly, then turns the steering wheel as the officer says again, “get out of the car.”

Almost simultaneously, Becca Good, standing in the street, shouts: “Drive, baby, drive!”

One officer standing in front of the vehicle pulls his weapon and fires into the windshield. He lurches back as the car turns away from him. The officer, who is now very close to the open window on the driver’s side, opens fire two more times, fatally shooting Renee Good, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.

Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense and that Good had engaged in “an act of domestic terrorism.”

The lawsuit against the United States of America seeks damages for Good's wrongful death and “the immense suffering Renee endured in the final moments of her life and for the profound and permanent losses that her death has inflicted upon her family,” according to a news release filed by lawyers for Ganger and Good.

The lawsuit also alleges “intentional infliction of emotional distress and negligent infliction of emotional distress” on Becca Good.

Becca and Renee Good were not legally married, according to a family lawyer, but referred to one another as wives. They had only recently relocated to Minneapolis from Kansas City, Missouri. It asks for a bench trial.

The other lawsuit alleges a conspiracy to interfere with civil rights and seeks a jury trial.

It says the shots fired by Jonathan Ross, the immigration officer who killed Good, “were the predictable and intended product of the operation,” which the lawsuit describes as a “carefully planned, coordinated effort between senior federal officials and private actors to make two ethnic communities — Minnesotans of Somali and Hispanic descent and origin — the object of aggression and abduction, and to silence by intimidation, arrest and violence the neighbors and allies of those targeted communities who observed, documented and warned of that campaign,” according to the news release.

The lawsuit also alleges “collaboration of federal agencies and individuals with private entities for an operation with discriminatory design, racially targeted pursuit and seizure of individuals without regard to their legal status, and each defendant’s participation in the conspiracy.”

It names Ross as a defendant, as well as: White House Deputy Chief of Staff Stephen Miller; former Homeland Security head Kristi Noem; former U.S. Border Patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino; Corey Lewandowski, President Donald Trump’s campaign manager, and others.

The killing of Good and another U.S. citizen, Alex Pretti, in Minneapolis just weeks later sparked outrage across the country and calls to rein in immigration enforcement. At least 10 people have died in encounters with immigration officers during President Donald Trump’s second term.

In social media accounts, Renee Good described herself as a “poet and writer and wife and mom.” On Pinterest, a profile picture shows her smiling and holding a young child, alongside posts about tattoos, hairstyles and home decorating.

In an interview shortly after her death, Renee Good’s mother, Donna Ganger, told The Associated Press: “She had this way of making you feel special and loved that I didn’t even understand that until we lost her.”

“As we have tried to navigate our own massive loss, I am also devastated by how many other lives have been destroyed in this darkest of times,” Becca Good said in the news release Thursday. “So many other families are dealing with the loss of their loved ones; to everyone who has had to witness it — the pain of this moment extends far beyond our family. What happened to us should never happen to any family.”

McCormack reported from Concord, New Hampshire.

entries.title: DoorDash Apologizes for Siding With GOP Bill Targeting D.C.
entries.summary: The company still wants the D.C. Council to make changes to a new delivery fee taking effect Thursday.
entries.content:
Food delivery company DoorDash says it is pulling its support for a Republican bill in Congress that would have limited D.C.’s ability to write its own tax laws, walking back a position that angered the city’s elected officials and prompted widespread calls for residents to boycott the service.

In a statement provided to The Washington Sun, Max Rettig, DoorDash’s head of global public policy, conceded that the company’s advocacy for the Republican bill was the wrong way to express its concerns with a new delivery fee imposed by the D.C. Council that takes effect Thursday.

“We recognize that working directly with District leaders is the right way to fight for District residents, and that doing otherwise calls into question our commitment to D.C.,” he said.

The political dustup started over the summer, when the council voted to impose a new 20-cent fee on all third-party deliveries. DoorDash unsuccessfully fought the fee in the Wilson Building, but also wrote a letter in support of a bill from Rep. James Comer (R-Kentucky) that would have required congressional approval for any tax or fee increases approved by the city’s lawmakers.

“We believe this is a reasonable check against the hastily enacted local taxes and fees that fall hardest on small businesses and the residents who depend on them,” John Horton, the company’s head of North American policy, wrote in the letter.

Comer’s bill — which was approved by the House Oversight Committee but has since stalled — drew furious condemnation from D.C.’s elected officials, including D.C. Council Chairman Phil Mendelson, who argued that it would impose a “straightjacket on District governance” and “paralyze our tax code.”

Many of those same officials said they were “stunned” that DoorDash supported the bill, given that it touched on an area of particular local sensitivity: increased Republican intervention in local affairs, whether led by the White House or Congress.

In response, Free DC — an advocacy group that has spearheaded protests against Republican interference in the city’s local affairs — launched a campaign encouraging residents to stop using the service.

“This bill is a blatant attack on D.C.’s power in order to support Trump’s grotesque desire to take over the capital,” it said of Comer’s measure.

Free DC also demanded that DoorDash publicly oppose Trump’s immigration enforcement efforts, which have impacted delivery drivers in D.C. and other cities. Relatedly, in June, a Venezuelan migrant working for DoorDash was killed when he was hit by a driver being chased by the U.S. Park Police.

In his statement, Rettig reiterated that DoorDash supports the city’s ability to govern itself. He also said that the company was investing $1 million to help local restaurants and would contribute 500,000 free meals to residents in 2027.

But Rettig also reiterated his hope that the council would work to exempt recipients of Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits from paying the new delivery fee. According to DoorDash, in 2025 it made 150,000 deliveries to SNAP beneficiaries in D.C., and more than 20% of its deliveries in the city went to low-income communities.

"Our letter of support for [Comer’s bill] came from a place of deep concern about this tax, particularly for D.C.'s most vulnerable residents,” he said. “The delivery tax disproportionately harms SNAP recipients who use these benefits to put food on the table and those with mobility issues, including seniors, who rely on delivery for their groceries and meals.”

Ward 1 Council member Brianne Nadeau, who included the new fee in the city’s 2027 budget, brushed aside those concerns over the summer, saying that revenue raised from the fee would help restore funding for food-assistance and grocery-delivery programs for low-income residents that would otherwise be cut.

entries.title: Ted Cruz’s Bid to Pass His College Sports Bill Soon Is Falling Short
entries.summary: Steve Scalise says the House game plan includes making changes — after the elections.
entries.content:
PORTSMOUTH, New Hampshire — It turns out the U.S. House of Representatives will not jump through hoops to vote on Sen. Ted Cruz’s college sports bill during the campaign season. After the midterms, the House might even try to call some audibles with the legislation.

The Texas Republican has been adamant the House could come back before the elections and quickly pass the Protect College Sports Act (or PCSA). But House Majority Leader Steve Scalise told The Washington Sun in an interview on Wednesday the House has a different plan that could include changes to Cruz’s proposal, which passed the Senate Monday with a large bipartisan majority.

“There's some good elements in the bill, but you saw there were some other problems that a number of our chairmen of the committees of jurisdiction in the House have with that bill, that would need to be fixed,” Scalise said. “Look, we've got our own process. We want to make sure we get this right, because it's really important that we allow the schools to govern themselves.”

Without delving into specifics, the Louisiana lawmaker said that while there are “differences between the House and the Senate” versions of the legislation, “there's a path to get a final bill to the president's desk, which is what we ultimately want.”

The differences are likely going to be “addressed in some amendments that will keep the focus of the bill on letting the schools govern themselves,” he said.

“That's what brought us all to the table,” Scalise said. “Have strong antitrust protections for schools to be able to govern themselves, so that courts don't overrule the decisions made by the schools, and you have people playing in their fifth and sixth and seventh year at their fourth school. And they're not getting an education because they're not even getting transferable credits. I mean, nobody wants that. We can fix it, and we're going to.”

A main function of the PCSA is that it would grant the NCAA and its sports conferences antitrust protection to set rules on athlete compensation, eligibility and the transfer portal. If the House were to change the bill through the amendment process in the lame-duck session after the midterms, it would have to go back to the Senate, further complicating its chance of passage.

There’s also no guarantee the House could pass any version of this bill, which Cruz co-authored with Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-Washington). Over the course of the past year, House leadership has had to pull their version of name, image and likeness legislation — known as the SCORE Act — from the floor due to opposition that would’ve tanked the bill. The PCSA would likely face a similar fate as written.

A source with knowledge of the matter told The Sun that a main issue the House GOP Conference has with the bill is that it does not prevent athletes from gaining employee status, which some Republicans believe could lead to unionization.

The SCORE Act barred college athletes from becoming employees, which has long been a goal of the NCAA. The PCSA, however, is neutral on employment, even if labor advocates believe its antitrust protections for the NCAA and conferences would stunt future organizing efforts.

In June, right after the PCSA was first introduced in the Senate, Scalise told Politico: “For the House to be able to take anything up, you got to prevent employment status of the student athletes.”

Another issue Republicans in the conference have with the PCSA is that it doesn’t impose limits on athletic scholarships for international athletes, the source added. Earlier this month, Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio) and Rep. Tim Walberg (R-Michigan) introduced a bill that would cap the number of roster spots each college team could offer to international athletes at 20%. Walberg chairs the House’s Education and Workforce Committee, which was very involved in crafting the SCORE Act in 2025.

If House Republicans insist on adding an employment ban to this bill, that could affect support among Democrats in the Senate. Cantwell fought hard for the PCSA to avoid the employment question, according to multiple Senate aides familiar with the negotiations. The talks included months of discussions between Cantwell and Cruz, plus Sens. Eric Schmitt (R-Missouri) and Chris Coons (D-Delaware), who are both co-sponsors. And along with Coons, Cantwell built a strong coalition of Democrats for the PCSA, getting 27 yeses from her party in the final vote Monday. (The overall tally was 77-22.)

To support the bill, those Democrats all broke with the AFL-CIO, which vehemently opposes the legislation. A full-on employment restriction, though, would conceivably be a no-go for many Democratic backers.

Employment isn’t the only issue the House could take a closer look at.

The PCSA’s provisions on conference expansion and realignment have also raised concern, particularly among Senators and House members from Florida. Those politicians are generally trying to make it so schools such as Florida State and the University of Miami maintain the flexibility to switch conferences if the opportunity arises in the near future.

It is already a sprawling bill, up to 180 pages after the Senate added amendments before the final vote. Shortly after it passed, Tim Buckley, the NCAA’s senior vice president for external affairs, sent a memo to schools, which The Sun obtained. The message was for school leaders to keep the pressure on their senators and representatives to push the PCSA through the House.

“Over the next few weeks, your continued advocacy is essential to keep up the momentum,” Buckley wrote. “The message is clear: Pass the PCSA as drafted as soon as possible. Amending the bill at this point would almost certainly make it impossible to get it to the President’s desk this Congress.”

But, as Scalise described, the House likely plans to take its turn with the ball first.

entries.title: The Mystics’ Championship Window Is Now Open
entries.summary: Even after a tough playoff exit, Washington is set up to contend for a title. “We want to be that team — next year, the year after,” coach Sydney Johnson says.
entries.content:
At the end of a season of development and growth, when the impossibly youthful and joyful Washington Mystics learned to crawl, then walk, then run together, there was one more new experience to navigate, one last lesson to learn: how to say goodbye to something you never imagined ending.

After the final buzzer sounded Wednesday night at CareFirst Arena and their 93-75 loss to the Atlanta Dream was in the books, ending the Mystics’ season in the first round of the WNBA playoffs, Washington’s players staggered toward midcourt for a brief huddle, then repaired to their locker room to bid farewell to a season their coach would later call “magical” — and to each other.

In those raw moments, there was no consoling Shakira Austin, after she had gone hip to hip and elbow to sharp elbow with Atlanta’s Angel Reese for the previous two-plus hours and gotten the worse of it, with talk of how the Mystics had been playing with house money anyway. There was no solace for Kiki Iriafen in the fact the Mystics had arrived at an elite level ahead of schedule, altering the franchise’s trajectory. There was no silver lining for Sonia Citron in being reminded that the Mystics’ young core, of which she is an essential piece, is the envy of the league.

All there was, was emptiness.

“I get emotional,” Citron said, pausing to collect herself. “We have something special here. We love each other. We have fun. We never lose our joy. That’s super special. I don’t think that’s everywhere. And I’m just grateful.”
Sonia Citron (4209x2806, AR: 1.50)But even as they scatter to their home bases, many of them with domestic or overseas playing opportunities come this winter, these Mystics may at some point allow themselves the grace to step back and ponder both what they accomplished in 2026 and how they set up this franchise for even bigger things in future seasons.

“We can’t take this year for granted,” coach Sydney Johnson said. “We have to understand how we got here, and we have to recreate it and add to it. There’s only going to be one team that holds up the trophy, and we want to be that team — next year, the year after. That’s what we’re working for.”

The Mystics were not only the youngest team in the WNBA this season, but (at least until a late-season roster shuffle) the second-youngest in the history of the league, and later the youngest team ever to make the playoffs. At times Wednesday night, they deployed a lineup made up entirely of first- and second-year players.

“I don’t even recognize this team,” Johnson said. “Every single player has gotten better. They’re a different player than they were four or five months ago. And the youth of this team — to understand how we’re trying to win, it came so quickly.”

Even as the rest of the league took note of the Mystics’ talent — which included six first-round picks from the past two drafts — few expected them to make much noise in 2026. The WNBA’s own preseason power rankings had them ranked 12th in the 15-team league; ESPN’s had them 11th.

But after reaching mid-July with a .500 record, the Mystics went 16-4 the rest of the way to seize the fifth seed in the WNBA playoffs. Other teams marveled at the way they played on a nightly basis — with both extraordinary physicality in the paint (they led the league in rebounding by a healthy margin) and extraordinary chemistry on the bench and in the locker room.

“They’re really well-coached,” Dream coach Karl Smesko said. “They’re obviously very physical. And… they look like they have fun playing together. They got better in each part of the season that went by.”

This was supposed to be the year the Mystics’ rebuild reached and possibly turned the corner. Instead, it took that corner like a stock-car racer and accelerated down the straightaway — a sooner-than-expected arrival that now brings them to the familiar crossroads that confronts franchises when they reach the other side: Now what?

By accomplishing what they did this season, the Mystics have thrown open their championship window, and the organization has both the justification and the wherewithal to go big this offseason. At the least, there will almost certainly be one major addition, courtesy of the Chicago Sky.

In February 2025, the Mystics traded veteran guard Ariel Atkins to the Sky for a 2025 first-round draft pick (which became Citron), as well as a swap of first-round picks in 2026. That means the Mystics, instead of picking at the back of the pack based on their 2026 seeding, will get the Sky’s lottery pick, which, owing to the Sky’s 16-28 record (tied for 10th in the standings), could be anywhere from first to fifth in a draft deep with high-level talent — putting them in position to take someone like USC’s JuJu Watkins, Notre Dame’s Hannah Hidalgo or Madison Booker of Texas.

Free agency provides another, more expensive pathway, though the Mystics’ plethora of players on their rookie contracts affords them the luxury to spend big. What do the Mystics need from a roster-construction standpoint to take the next step in 2027 and beyond?

They will almost certainly aim to get better at point guard, whether that means trusting they can get more out of Georgia Amoore — a first-round pick in 2025 who missed all of that season with an ACL tear and thus played this season as a rookie — or looking outside. They could also use a guard or wing with a deadly three-point shot (having taken the fewest three-point attempts in the league this season).

Among the big names on the list of unrestricted free agents who could fit either or both criteria: Indiana’s Kelsey Mitchell, Phoenix’s Kelsey Plum or Jackie Young of the Las Vegas Aces, who, combined, own 15 All-Star nods and five WNBA titles. Meantime, the Mystics have just one unrestricted free agent: veteran wing Betnijah Laney-Hamilton, whom they picked up on a waiver claim in August.

Chemistry and culture are core philosophies of Monumental Basketball, the parent company for both the Mystics and Washington Wizards, and any potential acquisitions, especially one that might alter the molecular makeup of the locker room culture, will almost certainly be viewed through that lens.

The 2026 Mystics were as close-knit a team as you are likely to see — equal parts joy, love and toughness — and keeping that feeling intact while adding game-changing talent will be a challenge for the team’s brain trust, which, in the absence of a general manager, includes Monumental Senior Vice President John Thompson III, Monumental President Michael Winger and Johnson.

“For me to see them love and care for each other on and off the court is everything I could ask for,” Johnson said of his 2026 Mystics. “And we won games. This wasn’t some ‘Kumbaya’ thing going on. … We won games and played for each other. And were selfless and joyful. And I want the world to know, that’s how we roll in D.C. And you can win. So next year, we’re going to come back stronger and want more, but we’re also going to hold to our culture, which is toughness, togetherness and a little bit of love sprinkled in there.”

entries.title: The Washington Sun launches The Washington Sun Magazine
entries.summary: The Sun will work with Washingtonian to distribute an initial six-month run of a monthly print publication.
entries.content:
The Washington Sun is creating The Washington Sun Magazine, a monthly print publication featuring some of the most compelling journalism produced by The Sun’s newsroom, with an emphasis on longform storytelling, essays and local news. The magazine will also feature The Sun’s Hill reporting, D.C. sports and culture coverage, and opinion columnists.

The magazine, which will run for six editions, is being edited by Richard Just, who is also the editor of The Washington Sun’s Perspectives section and is the former editor of The Washington Post Magazine. The magazine’s deputy editor is Alexa McMahon, formerly of the Post Magazine, and the assistant editor is Anusha Mathur. The magazine is being designed by Erin Aulov, a former visuals editor and art director at Politico and National Journal. Reporters and editors from across The Sun’s newsroom contributed to creating the publication.

“The Washington Sun produces such incredible journalism, and we are proud to present that journalism in the form of a beautifully designed magazine,” Just said. “The magazine is both a great introduction to The Washington Sun as a whole and a D.C. magazine that, we hope, does what the best magazines do: offers people a thoughtful, entertaining, enlightening reading experience and a window onto the world around them.”

The magazine will be distributed across D.C., including to every Capitol Hill office. The first three issues will be distributed in partnership with Washingtonian to their subscribers.

“As we grow our team and expand our reach, we can’t think of a better partner than Washingtonian, which is truly a D.C. institution. We are proud to complement their lifestyle and service journalism with our news, politics and local coverage,” said The Washington Sun’s CEO Arielle Elliott.

The first issue features three longform stories (“Was a National Civics Competition Rigged?” “No ID, No Money, No Escape: One Man’s Deportation Nightmare,” and “The Era of the MAGA Waist”), plus columns by Dana Milbank and Matt K. Lewis; Tom Sietsema on Ned’s Club; excerpts from interviews with House Speaker Mike Johnson, Rep. Sarah McBride, and Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed; a profile of a Nats player who never actually played; a statistical investigation of whether Marylanders are really the worst drivers in the DMV; and much more.

For press inquiries about The Washington Sun, email communications manager Thuy Lan Nguyen at thuylannguyen@washsun.com.

entries.title: White House Drops CNN From Trump’s Travel Press Pool Again
entries.summary: The move comes after a federal judge blocked the administration’s effort to more tightly control the media outlets that have access to the president.
entries.content:
The White House dropped CNN from the press pool covering President Donald Trump’s trip to Texas and Oklahoma on Thursday, a move that comes after a federal judge blocked the administration’s effort to more tightly control the media outlets that have access to the president.

CNN had been slated to travel on Air Force One and provide on-the-ground coverage, according to a schedule released Sunday by the White House. But updated guidance released Wednesday night had removed the network from that slot without explanation. No pool camera will travel with Trump, The Hill reported.

CNN confirmed its removal to NBC News.

It was the second time in less than a week that the White House kept CNN off a presidential travel pool. The network was also barred from flying with Trump to Tennessee over the weekend.

A federal judge last week ordered the White House to restore press credentials for CNN, MS NOW and Politico for 14 days. U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly found the outlets likely to succeed on their claim that the administration revoked their credentials without constitutionally adequate due process. The order covered access to White House grounds and did not specifically address travel with the president or TV pool assignments.

The outlets asked Kelly to extend the order while their lawsuit proceeds. CNN separately asked him to address the administration’s exclusion of the network from pool assignments. The Washington Sun has also signed onto an amicus brief filed in this case in support of the news outlets.

The administration’s response to the CNN filing is due Friday.

Trump imposed the ban last month, accusing the outlets of reporting “FICTION and LIES.” The ban drew condemnation from the White House Correspondents’ Association, and major television networks that rotate pool coverage also withheld coverage of Trump for several days in solidarity with the outlets.

In a Time magazine interview published Thursday, Trump suggested that he would continue to exclude the outlets and defended the restrictions, saying, “I haven't had a good story on CNN for years.”

Asked whether he was ignoring Kelly’s order, Trump said he was not, then added, “When they say orders, what order? I'm not even aware.” He called Kelly “a very anti-Trump judge.”

According to a transcript of the interview, White House communications director Steven Cheung interjected at one point that restoring the outlets’ White House credentials was a separate issue from allowing the networks to cover events aboard Air Force One or in the Oval office.
entries.author: Hamed Ahmadi

entries.title: Tennessee Governor Halts Executions After Botched Attempt
entries.summary: Officials were unable to put Christa Gail Pike to death Wednesday for a 1995 murder after administering two doses of a lethal drug.
entries.content:
By Kim Chandler and Kristin M. Hall

NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Tennessee officials were unable to put Christa Gail Pike to death Wednesday for a 1995 murder after administering two doses of a lethal drug. A death penalty expert said it was an unprecedented failure, and Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee halted the one remaining execution for the rest of the year.

Pike, 50, was alive and loudly snoring after the attempted lethal injection and taken by ambulance from the prison, her attorneys said. She was being treated at a hospital, but they said they hadn’t been told about her condition.

She had been scheduled for execution at 10 a.m. Wednesday for the killing she committed at age 18 and would have been the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years. An appeals court stopped the lethal injection just an hour before it was to start and hours later the U.S. Supreme Court overturned that stay.

Officials gave Pike two doses of pentobarbital, her attorneys said in court filings late Wednesday.

Gov. Bill Lee said in a statement that he has ordered “a comprehensive, third-party review to determine exactly what occurred” and that the remaining scheduled execution will not take place this year.

“Carrying out a lawfully imposed sentence is among the State’s most serious responsibilities, and the people of Tennessee expect it to be done in a manner that is not only legal and constitutional, but is effective,” he said.

The Tennessee Department of Correction said in a statement that it “followed every step of the State’s lawful, established execution protocol approved by the Attorney General’s Office.”

The state's execution protocol calls for a secondary set of drug syringes to be administered “if the inmate is not deceased” after the first set. It does not spell out what happens if the subject is alive after the second set.

Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said what Pike experienced is “singular and unparalleled.”

Seven other people have survived medical problems due to an execution team's failure to access a vein to administer lethal injection drugs, but no one has stayed alive after receiving the drugs used in such executions, she said.

Media witnesses detail the execution process

Media witnesses observing from a separate room said officials raised curtains to the execution chamber at 7:27 p.m., showing Pike strapped to a gurney.

“I’m going to leave this world the way I spent most of my life and that is in love,” she said in her “last” words. She described herself as at peace.

But Pike remained awake and at one point raised her head and asked prison officials if her arm was supposed to feel that way. It was not clear what she was referencing.

By 8:26 p.m., execution witnesses reported that the second dose of pentobarbital had been administered.

Pike continued to be heard snoring behind the closed curtain until the microphone was cut off at 8:53 p.m. At that time there was an announcement to escort media witnesses out of the area.

Lawyers for Pike filed an emergency motion late Wednesday to the Tennessee Supreme Court seeking to immediately halt and stay the execution, saying she was in “unnecessary agony” and it was violating her right to be executed free of cruel and unusual punishment. They also filed motions in the Sixth Circuit court and a district court.

It was the second time this year that Tennessee has been unable to carry out an execution: In May state officials called off the lethal injection of Tony Carruthers, who was convicted of kidnapping and killing three people in 1994, after executioners tried and failed for over an hour to place an IV to administer pentobarbital.

Pike and her boyfriend were convicted of the fatal stabbing and beating in 1995 of 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, their classmate at a job training facility in Knoxville. The case garnered widespread attention in part because of a pentagram that was carved on Slemmer’s body, and other elements of the crime stoked fears of Satan worship during the “satanic panic” of the 1980s and 1990s.

Stay of execution was swiftly appealed

Pike was initially scheduled to be put to death in the morning, and witnesses had gathered at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution in Nashville when the 6th Circuit U.S. Court of Appeals voted 2-1 to issue a stay. That court said a delay was needed to consider whether Pike’s allegations of childhood sexual abuse were fully considered at her sentencing.

The attorney general’s office appealed to the Supreme Court, saying that halting the execution at the last moment traumatized Slemmer’s family and rewarded “abusive delay tactics” by Pike’s attorneys.

Later in the day, the high court cleared the way for the execution to proceed. The conservative majority did not explain their order, while the three liberal members signed a dissent that said Pike’s claims deserved a closer look.

Pike did not deny committing the killing, but her supporters argued that the state should consider her age at the time, her mental illness and her allegations of severe sexual abuse.

Case renewed debate on the death penalty for teens

As the execution date drew near, debate renewed over the death penalty for young offenders.

Assistant Federal Defender Stephen Ferrell said Pike’s death sentence is an outlier because other 18-year-olds in Tennessee have had such sentences vacated.

After the killing, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder and post-traumatic stress disorder. In her clemency petition, she said she only wanted to fight Slemmer but killed her in a frenzied attack when she couldn’t “put the brakes on.”

“I was a mentally ill 18-year-old kid. It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in a statement.

Victim's mother says she is waiting for death sentence

Slemmer’s mother had traveled to Nashville in the hopes of witnessing the execution of her daughter’s killer. She told The Associated Press on Saturday that she had waited decades to see Pike’s sentence carried out.

“Every time I think about it, I think about Colleen feeling that pain and trying to get up and run,” May Martinez told The Associated Press in a telephone interview on Saturday.

Martinez could not be immediately reached by telephone for comment after the execution was halted.

The killing rocked the city of Knoxville. Prosecutors said Pike, fearing Slemmer was trying to steal her boyfriend, lured her to a wooded area on Jan. 12, 1995. Pike cut Slemmer with a box cutter and beat her with a large chunk of asphalt. Shipp, Pike’s boyfriend, has admitted that he was the one who carved a pentagram, a star-shaped symbol associated with Satan, into her body.

Shipp was 17 when the crime happened and received a sentence of life in prison with the possibility of parole. Pike was the only one sentenced to death.

Executions of women are rare in the US

Since the Supreme Court reinstated the death penalty in 1976, 18 women have been put to death, representing about 1% of all executions, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.

Pike would have been the 30th person executed in the U.S. this year after Florida carried out an execution on Tuesday.

Tennessee announced in 2024 that it was switching from a three-drug series for lethal injections to the single drug pentobarbital. That came more than two years after the state abruptly halted the execution of Oscar Smith and acknowledged that it had failed to ensure its lethal injection drugs were tested properly.

Associated Press writers Jeffrey Collins in Columbia, South Carolina, Ed White in Detroit, Hallie Golden in Seattle and Hannah Schoenbaum in Salt Lake City contributed.
entries.author: The Associated Press
